html:
This bar covers European colonial rule in Southeast Asia, from the Spanish conquest of the Philippines in 1565 to the independence of Malaya in 1957. By 1900 every country in the region except Siam was ruled by a European power or the United States.

It came in stages. First came trading posts and forts, then, from the 19th century, full territorial empires:

  • Spain took the Philippines from 1565, led by Legazpi, and ruled from Manila, linked to Mexico by the Manila galleons. The United States took over in 1898.
  • The Dutch, through the Dutch East India Company, made Batavia on Java their base in 1619 and slowly took over the archipelago. In the 19th century the Cultivation System forced Javanese farmers to grow export crops for the state.
  • Britain took Penang, then Singapore in 1819 under Raffles, divided the region with the Dutch in the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, conquered Burma in three wars ending in 1885, and took control of the Malay states.
  • France conquered Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos between 1858 and 1893 and joined them as French Indochina.

Siam survived as a buffer between British and French territory, helped by the reforms of King Chulalongkorn and by giving up border lands.

Colonial rule brought railways, ports, plantations of rubber, sugar and coffee, mines, and migrants from China and India. It also brought forced labour, famines and racial hierarchies, and it redrew borders that still stand. Japan's conquest of the region in 1941 and 1942 broke European prestige. After the war came the wave of independence, from Indonesia's declaration in 1945 to Malaya in 1957.
